conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is not well supported, clarifying that food-grade waxes used on apples are not carcinogenic and that exposure levels to any theoretical trace additives are negligible.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: The claim is not well supported.** Food-grade waxes used on apples (carnauba wax, shellac, beeswax, candelilla wax) are approved coating materials meant to replace the natural wax lost during washing, and there's no credible evidence these primary waxes themselves cause cancer (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/you-asked/why-do-they-spray-wax-apples-0; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruit_waxing).

The claim likely traces back to **morpholine**, an emulsifying additive sometimes used with wax on conventional apples, not the wax itself. Morpholine is a secondary amine that can react with dietary nitrites to form N-nitrosomorpholine, a compound classified as genotoxic/carcinogenic in rodent studies (https://x.com/SamaHoole/status/2081623670309454139; https://nontoxicdad.com/solutions/why-you-need-to-wash-the-wax-off-your-apples/). This concern led the EU to restrict morpholine-treated apple imports around 2010–2011 (https://goodfruit.com/european-rule-takes-the-shine-off-apples/).

However, McGill University's Office for Science and Society notes that the actual amount of morpholine left on apples is extremely small—only millionths of a gram per apple, since it is volatile and mostly evaporates during application (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/critical-thinking-health-and-nutrition/waxing-lyrical-about-fruit-wax). At these trace levels, the theoretical risk from nitrosamine formation is considered negligible by mainstream food-safety reviewers, even though regulatory caution (the EU restriction) exists.

**Bottom line:** "Wax causes cancer" is an oversimplification. The wax itself (carnauba, shellac, beeswax) is not carcinogenic. The narrower, more defensible concern is about morpholine, a minor additive in some conventional wax formulations, which theoretically could contribute trace carcinogenic nitrosamines—prompting EU restrictions—but exposure levels are very low and washing apples further reduces any residue.
